reasons: Lake identity lists case_name as Michigan v. DeFillippo, court as U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided as 1979-06-25, and year as 1979.
Lake citations list official cite 443 U.S. 31, parallel cites 99 S. Ct. 2627 and 61 L. Ed. 2d 343, and vendor neutral cite 1979 U.S. LEXIS 135.
The opinion frames the question as whether an arrest made in good-faith reliance on an ordinance not yet declared unconstitutional remains valid after later invalidation.

The opinion states that no deterrence purpose would be served by suppressing evidence from a lawful arrest and search where police enforced a presumptively valid statute, supporting placement under The Good-Faith Exception.
Lake progeny data reports substantial later citation activity, supporting a Key role.
residual_risks: The displayed Appears on section lists The Exclusionary Rule rather than The Good-Faith Exception, although the reviewed frontmatter home is supported.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Consider making the visible Appears on section match the frontmatter home, or label this case as a pre-Leon statutory-reliance/good-faith precursor if the taxonomy distinguishes precursors from progeny.

reasons: The opinion states: "On this record there was abundant probable cause to satisfy the constitutional prerequisite for an arrest."
The opinion states: "The subsequently determined invalidity of the Detroit ordinance on vagueness grounds does not undermine the validity of the arrest made for violation of that ordinance".
The proposition tracks the holding at the case-fact level: probable cause existed when officers enforced a presumptively valid ordinance, and later invalidation did not invalidate the arrest/search.
residual_risks: The short holding omits the Court's caveat for laws so grossly and flagrantly unconstitutional that reasonable officers would see the flaw.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add that there was no controlling precedent invalidating the ordinance and that the rule does not extend to grossly and flagrantly unconstitutional laws.
